wishing: a. & n. from Wish, v. t. Wishing bone. See Wishbone. -- Wishing cap, a cap fabled to give one whatever he wishes for when wearing it.
wishywashy: Thin and pale; weak; without strength or substance; -- originally said of liquids. Fig., weak-minded; spiritless. A weak wishy-washy man who had hardly any mind of his own. A. Trollope. | A weak or thin drink or liquor; wish-wash.
wivern: 1. (Her.) A fabulous two-legged, winged creature, like a cockatrice, but having the head of a dragon, and without spurs. [Written also wyvern.] The jargon of heraldry, its griffins, its mold warps, its wiverns, and its dragons. Sir W. Scott. 2. (Zoöl.) The weever.
wicked: Having a wick; -- used chiefly in composition; as, a two-wicked lamp. | 1. Evil in principle or practice; deviating from morality; contrary to the moral or divine law; addicted to vice or sin; sinful; immoral; profligate; -- said of persons and things; as, a wicked king;
witchuck: The sand martin, or bank swallow. [Prov. Eng.]
withers: The ridge between the shoulder bones of a horse, at the base of the neck. See Illust. of Horse. Let the galled jade wince; our withers are unwrung. Shak.
wince: 1. To shrink, as from a blow, or from pain; to flinch; to start back. I will not stir, nor wince, nor speak a word. Shak. 2. To kick or flounce when unsteady, or impatient at a rider; | A reel used in dyeing, steeping, or washing cloth; a winch. It is placed over the division wall between two wince pits so as to allow the cloth to descend into either compartment. at will.
wishful: 1. Having desire, or ardent desire; longing. 2. Showing desire; as, wishful eyes. From Scotland am I stolen, even of pure love To greet mine own land with my wishful sight. Shak. 3. Desirable; exciting wishes. Chapman. -- Wish"ful*ly, adv. -- Wish"ful*ness, n.
wieldsome: Admitting of being easily wielded or managed. (old) Golding.
wit: To know; to learn. "I wot and wist alway." Chaucer. Note: The present tense was inflected as follows; sing. 1st pers. wot; 2d pers. wost, or wot(t)est; 3d pers. wot, or wot(t)eth; pl. witen, or wite. | 1. Mind; intellect; understanding; sense. Who knew the wit of the Lord or who was his counselor Wyclif (Rom. xi. 34). A prince most prudent, of an excellent And unmatched wit and judgment. Shak.
witchery: 1. Sorcery; enchantment; witchcraft. Great Comus, Deep skilled in all his mother's witcheries. Milton. A woman infamous . . . for witcheries. Sir W. Scott. 2. Fascination; irresistible influence; enchantment. He never felt The witchery of the soft blue sky. Wordsworth. The dear, dear witchery of song. Bryant.
will: 1. The power of choosing; the faculty or endowment of the soul by which it is capable of choosing; the faculty or power of the mind by which we decide to do or not to do; | 1. To wish; to desire; to incline to have. A wife as of herself no thing ne sholde [should] Wille in effect, but as her husband wolde [would]. Chaucer. Caleb said unto her, What will thou Judg. i.
wickedly: In a wicked manner; in a manner, or with motives and designs, contrary to the divine law or the law of morality; viciously; corruptly; immorally. I have sinned, and I have done wickedly. 2 Sam. xxiv. 17.
widen: To make wide or wider; to extend in breadth; to increase the width of; as, to widen a field; to widen a breach; to widen a stocking. | To grow wide or wider; to enlarge; to spread; to extend. Arches widen, and long aisles extend. Pope.
widual: Of or pertaining to a widow; vidual. (old) Bale.
wicke: Wicked. (old) Piers Plowman. "With full wikke intent." Chaucer.
wiry: 1. Made of wire; like wire; drawn out like wire. 2. Capable of endurance; tough; sinewy; as, a wiry frame or constitution. "A little wiry sergeant of meek demeanor and strong sense." Dickens. He bore his age well, and seemed to retain a wiry vigor and alertness. Hawthorne.
winsome: 1. Cheerful; merry; gay; light-hearted. Misled by ill example, and a winsome nature. Jeffrey. 2. Causing joy or pleasure; gladsome; pleasant. Still plotting how their hungry ear That winsome voice again might hear. Emerson.
wildgrave: A waldgrave, or head forest keeper. See Waldgrave. The wildgrave winds his bugle horn. Sir W. Scott.
willier: One who works at a willying machine.
windbore: The lower, or bottom, pipe in a lift of pumps in a mine. Ansted.
winterly: Like winter; wintry; cold; hence, disagreeable, cheerless; as, winterly news. Shak. The sir growing more winterly in the month of April. Camden.
winter: 1. The season of the year in which the sun shines most obliquely upon any region; the coldest season of the year. "Of thirty winter he was old." Chaucer. And after summer evermore succeeds Barren… | To pass the winter; to hibernate; as, to winter in Florida. Because the haven was not commodious to winter in, the more part advised to depart thence. Acts xxvii. 12.
wildfire: 1. A composition of inflammable materials, which, kindled, is very hard to quench; Greek fire. Brimstone, pitch, wildfire . . . burn cruelly, and hard to quench. Bacon. 2. (Med.) (a) An old name for erysipelas. (b) A disease of sheep, attended with inflammation of the skin. 3. A sort of lightning unaccompanied by thunder.
withdrawment: The act of withdrawing; withdrawal. W. Belsham.
withal: 1. With this; with that. (old) He will scarce be pleased withal. Shak. 2. Together with this; likewise; at the same time; in addition; also. (old) Fy on possession But if a man be virtuous withal. | With; -- put after its object, at the end of sentence or clause in which it stands. (old) This diamond he greets your wife withal. Shak. Whatsoever uncleanness it be that a man shall be defiled…
windsucker: 1. (Far.) A horse given to wind-sucking Law. 2. (Zoöl.) The kestrel. B. Jonson.
wizened: Dried; shriveled; withered; shrunken; weazen; as, a wizened old man.
wiliness: The quality or state of being wily; craftiness; cunning; guile.
wiper: 1. One who, or that which, wipes. 2. Something used for wiping, as a towel or rag. 3. (Mach.) A piece generally projecting from a rotating or swinging piece, as an axle or rock shaft, for the purpose of raising stampers, lifting rods, or the like, and leaving them to fall by their own weight; a kind of cam. 4.
wirewoundgun: A gun in the construction of which an inner tube (either entire or in segments) is wound with wire under tension to insure greater soundness and uniformity of resistance. In modern construction hoops and jackets are shrunk on over the wire.
wildcat: 1. Unsound; worthless; irresponsible; unsafe; -- said to have been originally applied to the notes of an insolvent bank in Michigan upon which there was the figure of a panther. 2. (Railroad) Running without control; running along the line without a train; as, a wild-cat locomotive.
windle: 1. A spindle; a kind of reel; a winch. 2. (Zoöl.) The redwing. [Prov. Eng.]
wildly: In a wild manner; without cultivation; with disorder; rudely; distractedly; extravagantly.
winy: Having the taste or qualities of wine; vinous; as, grapes of a winy taste. Dampier.
willowweed: (a) A European species of loosestrife (Lysimachia vulgaris). (b) Any kind of Polygonum with willowlike foliage.
wincer: One who, or that which, winces, shrinks, or kicks.
wizen: To wither; to dry. [Prov. Eng. & Scot.] | Wizened; thin; weazen; withered. A little lonely, wizen, strangely clad boy. Dickens.
witchcraft: 1. The practices or art of witches; sorcery; enchantments; intercourse with evil spirits. 2. Power more than natural; irresistible influence. He hath a witchcraft Over the king in 's tongue. Shak.
willemite: A silicate of zinc, usually occurring massive and of a greenish yellow color, also in reddish crystals (troostite) containing manganese.
wistit: A small South American monkey; a marmoset. [Written also wistiti, and ouistiti.]
witherod: A North American shrub (Viburnum nudum) whose tough osierlike shoots are sometimes used for binding sheaves.
wincing: The act of washing cloth, dipping it in dye, etc., with a wince. Wincing machine. (a) A wince. Ure. (b) A succession of winces. See Wince. Knight.
willowwort: (a) Same as Willow-weed. (b) Any plant of the order Salicaceæ, or the Willow family.
wirepuller: One who pulls the wires, as of a puppet; hence, one who operates by secret means; an intriguer. Political wire-pullers and convention packers. Lowell.
witling: A person who has little wit or understanding; a pretender to wit or smartness. A beau and witing perished in the forming. Pope. Ye newspaper witlings! ye pert scribbling folks! Goldsmith.
wigwam: An Indian cabin or hut, usually of a conical form, and made of a framework of poles covered with hides, bark, or mats; -- called also tepee. [Sometimes written also weekwam.] Very spacious was the wigwam, Made of deerskin dressed and whitened, With the gods of the Dacotahs Drawn and painted on its curtains. Longfellow.
wild: 1. Living in a state of nature; inhabiting natural haunts, as the forest or open field; not familiar with, or not easily approached by, man; not tamed or domesticated; as, a wild boar; a wild ox; | An uninhabited and uncultivated tract or region; a forest or desert; a wilderness; a waste; as, the wilds of America; the wilds of Africa. then Libya first, of all her moisture drained, Became a…
winningness: The quality or state of being winning. "Winningness in style." J. Morley.
winker: 1. One who winks. Pope. 2. A horse's blinder; a blinker.
winger: One of the casks stowed in the wings of a vessel's hold, being smaller than such as are stowed more amidships. Totten.
witherite: Barium carbonate occurring in white or gray six-sided twin crystals, and also in columnar or granular masses.
wizenfaced: Having a shriveled, thin, withered face.
winning: Attracting; adapted to gain favor; charming; as, a winning address. "Each mild and winning note." Keble. | 1. The act of obtaining something, as in a contest or by competition. 2. The money, etc., gained by success in competition or contest, esp, in gambling; -- usually in the plural.
wiltoncarpet: A kind of carpet woven with loops like the Brussels, but differing from it in having the loops cut so as to form an elastic velvet pile; -- so called because made originally at Wilton, England.
windlace: See Windlass. (old) Two arblasts, . . . with windlaces and quarrels. Sir W. Scott.
wigg: A kind of raised seedcake. "Wiggs and ale." Pepys.
winze: A small shaft sunk from one level to another, as for the purpose of ventilation.
winglet: 1. A little wing; a very small wing. 2. (Zoöl.) A bastard wing, or alula.
wireworm: (a) One of the larvæ of various species of snapping beetles, or elaters; -- so called from their slenderness and the uncommon hardness of the integument. Wireworms are sometimes very destructive to the roots of plants. Called also wire grub. (b) A galleyworm.
winterweed: A kind of speedwell (Veronica hederifolia) which spreads chiefly in winter. Dr. Prior.
wilding: A wild or uncultivated plant; especially, a wild apple tree or crab apple; also, the fruit of such a plant. Spenser. Ten ruddy wildings in the wood I found. Dryden. The fruit of the tree . . . | Not tame, domesticated, or cultivated; wild. (poetic) "Wilding flowers." Tennyson. The ground squirrel gayly chirps by his den, And the wilding bee hums merrily by. Bryant.
winnow: 1. To separate, and drive off, the chaff from by means of wind; to fan; as, to winnow grain. Ho winnoweth barley to-night in the threshing floor. Ruth. iii. 2. 2. | To separate chaff from grain. Winnow not with every wind. Ecclus. v. 9.
winterproud: Having too rank or forward a growth for winter. When either corn is winter-proud, or other plants put forth and bud too early. Holland.
windlass: A winding and circuitous way; a roundabout course; a shift. | To take a roundabout course; to work warily or by indirect means. (old) Hammond.
wiring: 1. The act of one that wires anything. 2. The wires or conductors employed in a system of electric distribution.
wiseacre: 1. A learned or wise man. (old) Pythagoras learned much . . . becoming a mighty wiseacre. Leland. 2. One who makes undue pretensions to wisdom; a would-be-wise person; hence, in contempt, a simpleton; a dunce.
witstarved: Barren of wit; destitute of genius. Examiner.
wilderment: The state of being bewildered; confusion; bewilderment. And snatched her breathless from beneath This wilderment of wreck and death. Moore.
withdrawer: One who withdraws; one who takes back, or retracts.
wight: 1. A whit; a bit; a jot. (old) She was fallen asleep a little wight. Chaucer. 2. A supernatural being. (old) Chaucer. 3. A human being; a person, either male or female; | Swift; nimble; agile; strong and active. [Obs. or Poetic] 'T is full wight, God wot, as is a roe. Chaucer. He was so wimble and so wight. Spenser. They were Night and Day, and Day and Night, Pilgrims…
windowpane: 1. (Arch.) See Pane, n., (3) b. [In this sense, written also window pane.] 2. (Zoöl.) A thin, spotted American turbot (Pleuronectes maculatus) remarkable for its translucency. It is not valued as a food fish. Called also spotted turbot, daylight, spotted sand flounder, and water flounder.
wike: A temporary mark or boundary, as a bough of a tree set up in marking out or dividing anything, as tithes, swaths to be mowed in common ground, etc.; -- called also wicker. [Prov. Eng.] | A home; a dwelling. [Obs. or Prov. Eng.]
widgeon: Any one of several species of fresh-water ducks, especially those belonging to the subgenus Mareca, of the genus Anas. The common European widgeon (Anas penelope) and the American widgeon (A. Americana) are the most important species. The latter is called also baldhead, baldpate, baldface, baldcrown, smoking duck, wheat, duck, and whitebelly.
wittol: 1. (Zoöl.) The wheatear. [Prov. Eng.] 2. A man who knows his wife's infidelity and submits to it; a tame cuckold; -- so called because the cuckoo lays its eggs in the wittol's nest. (old) Shak.
wigwag: To signal by means of a flag waved from side to side according to a code adopted for the purpose. [Colloq.]
windhover: The kestrel; -- called also windbibber, windcuffer, windfanner. [Prov. Eng.]
willful: 1. Of set purpose; self-determined; voluntary; as, willful murder. Foxe. In willful poverty chose to lead his life. Chaucer. Thou to me Art all things under heaven, all places thou, Who, for my willful crime, art banished hence. Milton. 2. Governed by the will without yielding to reason; obstinate; perverse; inflexible; stubborn; refractory; as, a willful man or horse.
wing: 1. One of the two anterior limbs of a bird, pterodactyl, or bat. They correspond to the arms of man, and are usually modified for flight, but in the case of a few species of birds, as the ostrich,… | 1. To furnish with wings; to enable to fly, or to move with celerity. Who heaves old ocean, and whowings the storms. Pope. Living, to wing with mirth the weary hours. Longfellow. 2.
witan: Lit., wise men; specif. (A.-S. Hist.), the members of the national, or king's, council which sat to assist the king in administrative and judicial matters; also, the council.
withy: 1. (Bot.) The osier willow (Salix viminalis). See Osier, n. (a). 2. A withe. See Withe, 1. | Made of withes; like a withe; flexible and tough; also, abounding in withes. The stream is brimful now, and lies high in this little withy plantation. G. Eliot.
winder: 1. One who, or that which, winds; hence, a creeping or winding plant. 2. An apparatus used for winding silk, cotton, etc., on spools, bobbins, reels, or the like. 3. | To fan; to clean grain with a fan. [Prov. Eng.]
wishbone: The forked bone in front of the breastbone in birds; -- called also merrythought, and wishing bone. See Merrythought, and Furculum.
wife: 1. A woman; an adult female; -- now used in literature only in certain compounds and phrases, as alewife, fishwife, goodwife, and the like. " Both men and wives." Piers Plowman. On the green he saw sitting a wife. Chaucer. 2. The lawful consort of a man; a woman who is united to a man in wedlock; a woman who has a husband; a married woman; -- correlative of husband.
wisket: A whisket, or basket. [Prov. Eng.] Ainsworth.
wingleaved: Having pinnate or pinnately divided leaves.
withstander: One who withstands, or opposes; an opponent; a resisting power.
withinforth: Within; inside; inwardly. (old) Wyclif. [It is much greater] labor for to withinforth call into mind, without sight of the eye withoutforth upon images, what he before knew and thought upon. Bp. Peacock.
wilfleytable: An inclined percussion table, usually with longitudinal grooves in its surface, agitated by side blows at right angles to the flow of the pulp; -- so called after the inventor.
wisdomliterature: The class of ancient Hebrew writings which deal reflectively with general ethical and religious topics, as distinguished from the prophetic and liturgical literature, and from the law. It is comprised chiefly in the books of Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiasticus, Ecclesiastes, and Wisdom of Solomon.
witless: Destitute of wit or understanding; wanting thought; hence, indiscreet; not under the guidance of judgment. "Witless bravery." Shak. A witty mother! witless else her son. Shak. Witless pity breedeth fruitless love. Fairfax. -- Wit"less*ly, adv. -- Wit"less*ness, n.
wikiup: The hut used by the nomadic Indian tribes of the arid regions of the west and southwest United States, typically elliptical in form, with a rough frame covered with reed mats or grass or brushwood.
wiretailed: Having some or all of the tail quills terminated in a long, slender, pointed shaft, without a web or barbules.
wincopipe: A little red flower, no doubt the pimpernel, which, when it opens in the morning, is supposed to bode a fair day. See Pimpernel. There is small red flower in the stubble fields, which country people call the wincopipe; which if it opens in the morning, you may be sure a fair day will follow. Bacon.
withering: Tending to wither; causing to shrink or fade. -- With"er*ing*ly, adv.
windjammer: 1. (Naut.) A sailing vessel or one of its crew; -- orig. so called contemptuously by sailors on steam vessels. [Colloq.] 2. An army bugler or trumpeter; any performer on a wind instrument. [Slang]
wilt: To begin to wither; to lose freshness and become flaccid, as a plant when exposed when exposed to drought, or to great heat in a dry day, or when separated from its root; to droop;. to wither. [Prov. | 1. To cause to begin to wither; to make flaccid, as a green plant. [Prov. Eng. U. S.] 2. Hence, to cause to languish; to depress or destroy the vigor and energy of. [Prov. Eng. & U.
wimple: 1. A covering of silk, linen, or other material, for the neck and chin, formerly worn by women as an outdoor protection, and still retained in the dress of nuns. Full seemly her wympel ipinched is. | 1. To clothe with a wimple; to cover, as with a veil; hence, to hoodwink. "She sat ywympled well." Chaucer. This wimpled, whining, purblind, wayward boy. Shak. 2. To draw down, as a veil;
widowmaker: One who makes widows by destroying husbands. Shak.
witenagemote: A meeting of wise men; the national council, or legislature, of England in the days of the Anglo-Saxons, before the Norman Conquest.
withdrawingroom: A room for retirement from another room, as from a dining room; a drawing-room. A door in the middle leading to a parlor and withdrawing-room. Sir W. Scott.
wideness: 1. The quality or state of being wide; breadth; width; great extent from side to side; as, the wideness of a room. "I landed in a small creek about the wideness of my canoe." Swift. 2. Large extent in all directions; broadness; greatness; as, the wideness of the sea or ocean.
windowy: Having little crossings or openings like the sashes of a window. Donne.
windless: 1. Having no wind; calm. 2. Wanting wind; out of breath.
wittified: Possessed of wit; witty. R. North.
wich: 1. A street; a village; a castle; a dwelling; a place of work, or exercise of authority; -- now obsolete except in composition; as, bailiwick, Warwick, Greenwick. Stow. 2. (Curling) A narrow port or passage in the rink or course, flanked by the stones of previous players.
widegap: The angler; -- called also widegab, and widegut.
winery: A place where grapes are converted into wine.
winterbeaten: Beaten or harassed by the severe weather of winter. Spenser.
winged: 1. Furnished with wings; transported by flying; having winglike expansions. 2. Soaring with wings, or as if with wings; hence, elevated; lofty; sublime. How winged the sentiment that virtue is to be followed for its own sake. J. S. Harford. 3. Swift; rapid. "Bear this sealed brief with winged haste to the lord marshal." Shak. 4. Wounded or hurt in the wing. 5.
winterground: To coved over in the season of winter, as for protection or shelter; as, to winter-ground the roods of a plant. The ruddock would . . . bring thee all this, Yea, and furred moss besides, when flowers are none To winter-ground thy corse. Shak.
wiredrawer: One who draws metal into wire.
widely: 1. In a wide manner; to a wide degree or extent; far; extensively; as, the gospel was widely disseminated by the apostles. 2. Very much; to a great degree or extent; as, to differ widely in opinion.
window: 1. An opening in the wall of a building for the admission of light and air, usually closed by casements or sashes containing some transparent material, as glass, and capable of being opened and shut… | 1. To furnish with windows. 2. To place at or in a window. Wouldst thou be windowed in great Rome and see Thy master thus with pleach'd arms, bending down His corrigible neck Shak.
windsignal: In general, any signal announcing information concerning winds, and esp. the expected approach of winds whose direction and force are dangerous to shipping, etc. The wind-signal system of the United States Weather Bureau consists of storm, information, hurricane, hot wind, and inland storm signals.
witsnapper: One who affects repartee; a wit-cracker. (old) Shak.
wicking: the material of which wicks are made; esp., a loosely braided or twisted cord or tape of cotton.
widowwail: A low, narrowleaved evergreen shrub (Cneorum tricoccon) found in Southern Europe.
windrode: Caused to ride or drive by the wind in opposition to the course of the tide; -- said of a vessel lying at anchor, with wind and tide opposed to each other. Totten.
withdrawal: The act of withdrawing; withdrawment; retreat; retraction. Fielding.
wideangle: Having or covering an angle wider than the ordinary; -- applied to certain lenses of relatively short focus. Lenses for ordinary purposes have an angle of 50º or less. Wide-angle lenses may cover as much as 100º and are useful for photographing at short range, but the pictures appear distorted.
witwall: (a) The golden oriole. (b) The greater spotted woodpecker. [Prov. Eng.]
windbreak: To break the wind of; to cause to lose breath; to exhaust. 'T would wind-break a mule to vie burdens with her. Ford. | A clump of trees serving for a protection against the force of wind. [Local, U. S.]
wiseling: One who pretends to be wise; a wiseacre; a witling. Donne.
witts: Tin ore freed from earthy matter by stamping. Knight.
willowherb: A perennial herb (Epilobium spicatum) with narrow willowlike leaves and showy rose-purple flowers. The name is sometimes made to include other species of the same genus. Spiked willow-herb, a perennial herb (Lythrum Salicaria) with willowy leaves and spiked purplish flowers.
wingfish: A sea robin having large, winglike pectoral fins. See Sea robin, under Robin.
withwind: A kind of bindweed (Convolvulus arvensis). He bare a burden ybound with a broad list, In a withewyndes wise ybounden about. Piers Plowman.
witty: 1. Possessed of wit; knowing; wise; skillful; judicious; clever; cunning. (old) "The deep-revolving witty Buckingham." Shak. 2. Especially, possessing wit or humor; good at repartee; droll; facetious; sometimes, sarcastic; as, a witty remark, poem, and the like. "Honeycomb, who was so unmercifully witty upon the women." Addison. Syn. -- Acute; smart; sharp; arch; keen;
willingness: The quality or state of being willing; free choice or consent of the will; freedom from reluctance; readiness of the mind to do or forbear. Sweet is the love which comes with willingness. Dryden.
wizardry: The character or practices o "He acquired a reputation bordering on wizardry." J. A. Symonds.
wistaria: A genus of climbing leguminous plants bearing long, pendulous clusters of pale bluish flowers. Note: The species commonest in cultivation is the Wistaria Sinensis from Eastern Asia. W. fruticosa grows wild in the southern parts of the United States.
with: With denotes or expresses some situation or relation of nearness, proximity, association, connection, or the like. It is used especially: -- 1. To denote a close or direct relation of opposition or hostility; - - equivalent to against. Thy servant will . . . fight with this Philistine. 1 Sam. xvii. 32.
within: 1. In the inner or interior part of; inside of; not without; as, within doors. O, unhappy youth! Come not within these doors; within this roof The enemy of all your graces lives. Shak. | 1. In the inner part; inwardly; internally. "The wound festers within." Carew. Ills from within thy reason must prevent. Dryden. 2. In the house; in doors; as, the master is within.
withsay: To contradict; to gainsay; to deny; to renounce. (old) Gower. If that he his Christendom withsay. Chaucer.
windbound: prevented from sailing, by a contrary wind. See Weatherbound.
witherling: A withered person; one who is decrepit. (old) Chapman.
widmanstattenfigures: Certain figures appearing on etched meteoric iron; -- so called after A. B. Widmanstätten, of Vienna, who first described them in 1808. See the Note and Illust. under Meteorite.
wingmanship: Power or skill in flying. Duke of Argyll.
wistful: 1. Longing; wishful; desirous. Lifting up one of my sashes, I cast many a wistful, melancholy look towards the sea. Swift. 2. Full of thought; eagerly attentive; meditative; musing; pensive; contemplative. That he who there at such an hour hath been, Will wistful linger on that hallowed spot. Byron. -- Wist"ful*ly, adv. -- Wist"ful*ness, n.
witted: Having (such) a wit or understanding; as, a quick-witted boy.
wineglassful: As much as a wineglass will hold; enough to fill a wineglass. It is usually reckoned at two fluid ounces, or four tablespoonfuls.
wichitas: A tribe of Indians native of the region between the Arkansas and Red rivers. They are related to the Pawnees. See Pawnees.
wisse: To show; to teach; to inform; to guide; to direct. (old) Ere we depart I shall thee so well wisse That of mine house ne shalt thou never misse. Chaucer.
widowhood: 1. The state of being a widow; the time during which a woman is widow; also, rarely, the state of being a widower. Johnson clung to her memory during a widowhood of more than thirty years. Leslie Stephen. 2. Estate settled on a widow. (old) "I 'll assure her of her widowhood . . . in all my lands." Shak.
wiver: 1. (Her.) A fabulous two-legged, winged creature, like a cockatrice, but having the head of a dragon, and without spurs. [Written also wyvern.] The jargon of heraldry, its griffins, its mold warps, its wiverns, and its dragons. Sir W. Scott. 2. (Zoöl.) The weever.
wile: A trick or stratagem practiced for insnaring or deception; a sly, insidious; artifice; a beguilement; an allurement. Put on the whole armor of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of… | 1. To practice artifice upon; to deceive; to beguile; to allure. Spenser. 2. To draw or turn away, as by diversion; to while or while away; to cause to pass pleasantly. Tennyson.
wimble: An instrument for boring holes, turned by a handle. Specifically: (a) A gimlet. " It is but like the little wimble, to let in the greater auger." Selden. (b) A stonecutter's brace for boring holes in… | To bore or pierce, as with a wimble. "A foot soldier . . . wimbled also a hole through said coffin." Wood.
windshaken: Shaken by the wind; specif. (Forestry), affected by wind shake, or anemosis (which see, above).
wielder: One who wields or employs; a manager; a controller. A wielder of the great arm of the war. Milton.
winnebagoes: A tribe of North American Indians who originally occupied the region about Green Bay, Lake Michigan, but were driven back from the lake and nearly exterminated in 1640 by the IIlinnois.
withe: 1. A flexible, slender twig or branch used as a band; a willow or osier twig; a withy. 2. A band consisting of a twig twisted. 3. (Naut.) An iron attachment on one end of a mast or boom, with a ring,… | To bind or fasten with withes. You shall see him withed, and haltered, and staked, and baited to death. Bp. Hall.
wickerwork: A texture of osiers, twigs, or rods; articles made of such a texture.
windgall: A soft tumor or synovial swelling on the fetlock joint of a horse; -- so called from having formerly been supposed to contain air.
